text:
*Interview with Bastien Girard, établisseur, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Girard, thank you for waiting. You are from Le Locle?

GIRARD: Le Locle, yes. I am an établisseur. I buy movements and parts, assemble them, and sell the watches under my firm's name. Ask anyone in the trade.

MATTHEY: Will you tell me about the evening in order, beginning with dinner?

GIRARD: Dinner was dinner. Monnier had the repeater on the table and talked about it as if it were a child of his. I came to buy the rights to it, and he wanted a price I would not pay. We quarrelled about it, both of us, in front of everyone.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

GIRARD: I sat on alone in the dining room with the brandy. I was not in a good temper and did not want the salon.

MATTHEY: Do you recall the time when the temple struck ten?

GIRARD: I do. I had my watch out, as I always do. A merchant who does not notice time loses money. When the temple struck ten, my watch showed four minutes to ten.

MATTHEY: What did you do then?

GIRARD: I went out into the street to smoke. It was twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch. The cold is hard tonight, with old snow in the street, but I walk in the cold when I want to think. I stopped under the front windows of the house and stayed there.

MATTHEY: What were you smoking?

GIRARD: Brissagos. The cheap ones. The doctor says they are a disgrace to the chest, and he says it every time he sees one.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything from the house while you were under the windows?

GIRARD: The piano started up in the salon just as I lit my cigar. It was twenty-nine minutes past ten by my watch.

MATTHEY: Who was playing?

GIRARD: I could not say. I heard it through the glass. I only know it was the piano.

MATTHEY: When did it stop?

GIRARD: It stopped at eighteen minutes to eleven by my watch.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything else before it stopped?

GIRARD: At twenty-six minutes to eleven by my watch I heard faint quick bells from the master's window up above. The piano was playing all the while.

MATTHEY: Can you describe the bells?

GIRARD: Faint and quick, one after another, like little silver bells. I have listened to a repeater before. I have sold a good many.

MATTHEY: When did you go back into the house?

GIRARD: I came back into the house at fourteen minutes to eleven by my watch. The hall clock had just struck eleven, and its face showed two minutes past eleven. I went up to Félix in the library.

MATTHEY: Why did you go up to Monsieur Félix?

GIRARD: He owes me money. I wanted to speak to him about it while I was in the house. That is all I will say about it, Inspector, and it is no business of anyone's but ours.

MATTHEY: You do not care for Doctor Vauthier's company, I think.

GIRARD: I do not. He quotes Latin at a man as if he were reading him a sentence. He has never once asked me a question he wanted the answer to.

MATTHEY: Is there anything else you think I should know?

GIRARD: Only that I am a merchant, Inspector. I deal in time and in money, and I tell you what I read off my watch. I have nothing to hide from either.
